opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really important question, because there's a temptation in our field to believe that you can do everything in silico. And I don't think that's true, at least not yet, and maybe not ever entirely.

The way I think about it is that the computational platform is a kind of funnel. You start with an enormous design space, potentially millions or billions of candidate materials, and you use generative models to propose structures, then increasingly accurate but increasingly expensive simulations to filter them. Fast machine-learned surrogates come first, then something like DFT, maybe higher-level quantum chemistry or molecular dynamics for the most promising candidates. At each stage you throw away most of what you had. But at the bottom of that funnel, you still need to make the thing and test it. Simulation tells you what should work. The lab tells you what actually works.

And there are several reasons why the experiment is irreplaceable. One is that our simulations have systematic errors. DFT functionals have known failure modes, and force fields trained on DFT inherit them. Another is synthesizability. You can design a beautiful material on a computer that is completely impossible to make, or that only forms under conditions nobody can reach at scale. And third, real materials are messy. They have defects, grain boundaries, impurities, and they degrade over time in humid or acidic environments. A carbon capture sorbent has to survive thousands of cycles in real flue gas, not just look good at zero kelvin in a perfect crystal.

So we don't see experiments as just a final validation step. We see them as part of the learning loop. You make predictions, you test a batch of candidates, and the results, especially the failures, flow back into the models. That's active learning, or Bayesian experimental design, in the language I've used for a long time. The experiment is your most expensive and most informative query, so you should choose it very carefully to maximize what you learn, not only to confirm what you hoped.

We also partner closely with experimental groups and companies who have real labs and real domain expertise, because building that whole capability from scratch is very hard. Over time I think more of it becomes automated, with self-driving labs and robotic synthesis and high-throughput characterization, and then the loop between the model and the physical world gets much tighter and faster. That's the exciting part to me: an AI system that doesn't just predict but actually learns from nature by asking it questions.

So to summarize: computation massively shrinks the search space and makes you much smarter about which experiments to run, but the physical experiment remains the ground truth. You can't escape it, and honestly you shouldn't want to, because that's where the new information comes from.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I don't see them as separate things at all. There's a tendency, especially coming from the machine learning side, to think of the lab as a kind of oracle that you consult at the end, once the computation has done its job. I think that's completely backwards. For us, the physical experiments are part of the loop, not the end of it.

Let me explain why. Any model we build, whether it's a generative model proposing new structures or a surrogate predicting properties, is only as good as the data it has seen. And in materials, the data is sparse, it's noisy, and it's biased toward whatever people happened to synthesize in the past. So if you only optimize inside the model, you very quickly end up in regions where the model is confidently wrong. You get beautiful candidates on paper that cannot be made, or that are unstable, or that don't have the property you predicted. The experiment is what keeps you honest.

So the way I think about it is more like active learning, or really like the scientific method itself. The model proposes, we identify where our uncertainty is highest and where the potential payoff is highest, and those are the candidates we want to test in the lab. Then the results, including the failures, especially the failures, go back into the model. Each experiment is expensive, so you want every one to be maximally informative. That's really a question of experimental design, and it's something I find quite beautiful because it brings in Bayesian ideas that I've cared about for a long time.

There's also a more fundamental reason. Physics gives us very strong priors. Simulations, DFT, molecular dynamics, these encode real knowledge, but they also have approximations baked in. The experiment is the only place where reality actually pushes back. If your simulation and the lab disagree, that's not a nuisance, that's the most valuable signal you can get, because it tells you where your physics is incomplete.

And practically speaking, at CuspAI, the thing that excites me is closing that loop faster. If the cycle from hypothesis to synthesis to characterization takes months, the machine learning doesn't matter much. If you can bring that down, and automate parts of it, then suddenly the computational side and the experimental side start to compound each other. That's when I think you get genuine discovery rather than just very fast screening.

r001.rationale: It says experiments are part of the discovery loop: lab results feed back into the model, and CuspAI aims to close that loop faster.

astra-6.text:
I think physical experiments are essential, because ultimately you want to discover a material that works in the real world. A computational model can suggest something very promising, but you still have to ask: Can we synthesize it? Does it have the properties we predicted? And do those properties hold under the conditions where we actually want to use it?

So I see this as a loop. Computation helps us narrow down the possibilities and choose which experiments are most informative. The experimental results then help us improve the models and decide where to look next. A failed prediction can be quite valuable in that process, because it tells you where your model is missing something.

The ambition is to make that cycle much more efficient. You don’t want to synthesize and test every candidate, but you also don’t want to mistake a good simulation result for a successful material.

sol-6.1.text:
I think physical experiments are essential, because ultimately you want a material that works in the real world. A simulation can predict interesting properties, but it makes approximations, and it doesn’t necessarily tell you whether a material can be synthesized or how it behaves under practical conditions.

So the way I think about it is as a feedback loop. Computation helps you explore a very large space and select promising candidates. You then synthesize and test those candidates, and the experimental results feed back into the models. A failed prediction can be very informative: it tells you where your model is missing something.

The goal isn’t to replace experiments. It’s to make each experiment more useful, so that you learn faster and reach a useful material with fewer iterations.
